note: Short texts in our own words. Figures as given in the project brief; checking them against the source and the link check are still due before launch (PRD F-02.2a, F-02.3).

items.headline: This is as high as Earth goes.
items.body: The summit of Mount Everest stands about 8,849 m above sea level, higher than any other mountain. Yet another peak lies farther from the centre of the Earth.

pair.text: Its counterpart: the Challenger Deep, the lowest point of the oceans

items.headline: Everest would sink without a trace.
items.body: The deepest known point of the oceans lies in the Mariana Trench, about 10,935 m below the surface. Put Mount Everest in it and its summit would still be some 2 km under water.

pair.text: Its counterpart: Mount Everest, the highest mountain on Earth

items.headline: The Sahara only comes second.
items.body: No hot desert on Earth is larger; it stretches from the Atlantic to the Red Sea. The title of largest desert of all goes to a continent of ice.

pair.text: Its counterpart: Antarctica, the largest desert in the world

items.headline: The world’s largest desert is white.
items.body: What makes a desert is not heat but how little precipitation falls. Deep inside Antarctica hardly any snow arrives all year, which makes the frozen continent the largest desert on Earth.

pair.text: Its counterpart: the Sahara, the largest hot desert

items.headline: A lake almost five Eiffel Towers deep.
items.body: Lake Baikal is about 1,642 m deep, deeper than any other lake on Earth. By volume it is also the largest freshwater lake.

items.headline: A white patch you can see from space.
items.body: The largest salt flat on Earth lies in the high Andes. The bright, almost perfectly level surface stands out at once on satellite images.
